messages.subject: overfitting or the the Stdev for spatial.field is no longer important
messages.subject_clean: overfitting or the the Stdev for spatial.field is no longer important
messages.body_plain:
I"m new to Bayesian statistics, so please bear with me. I recently realized that the models I created using INLA and spTimer were over fitting my data. I subsequently dropped the spTimer analyses because INLA was more flexible.

I followed the advice given here: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/r-inla-discussion-group/cPU0iJA2UqY. As such, I used the following code to reduce overfitting:

local.inla.spde2.matern.new <http://local.inla.spde2.matern.new> = function(mesh, alpha=2, prior.pc.rho, prior.pc.sig)
{
  # Call inla.spde2.matern with range and standard deviation parametrization
  d = INLA:::inla.ifelse(inherits(mesh, "inla.mesh"), 2, 1)
  nu = alpha-d/2
  kappa0 = log(8*nu)/2
  tau0   = 0.5*(lgamma(nu)-lgamma(nu+d/2)-d/2*log(4*pi))-nu*kappa0
  spde   = inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh,
                             B.tau   = cbind(tau0,   nu,  -1),
                             B.kappa = cbind(kappa0, -1, 0))

  # Change prior information
  param = c(prior.pc.rho, prior.pc.sig)
  spde$f$hyper.default$theta1$prior = "pcspdega"
  spde$f$hyper.default$theta1$param = param
  spde$f$hyper.default$theta1$initial = log(prior.pc.rho[1])+1
  spde$f$hyper.default$theta2$initial = log(prior.pc.sig[1])-1

  # End and return
  return(invisible(spde))
}
sig0 = 0.001; rho0 = 3500

spde = local.inla.spde2.matern.new <http://local.inla.spde2.matern.new>(mesh, prior.pc.rho = c(rho0, 0.5), prior.pc.sig = c(sig0, 0.5))

But I've been trying to strike the right balance, but to no avail. If I run the model after changing the coordinates of the data points to km (or not), and use large values for sig0, that is > 0.1, and a rho0 of half the maximum distance between the points (which is 7423.778 km) or if I just use spde = inla.spde2.matern(mesh=mesh, alpha = 2), there is over fitting.  This also occurs for another model that I am running with points that are close (a spatio-temporal model), where the maximum distance between points is 0.36 km. For both models, the minimum distance is 0.

If I use very small values of sig0 of around 0.001 or lower it stops the over fitting or if rho0 values of <0.001 are used, it stops the over fitting but in both cases, the Stdev for spatial.field is no longer important (zero is included in credibility intervals). Also, a map of the spatial random field doesn't look correct. I assume that if these values are used it is similar to removing the spatial field, because the DIC values are only marginally higher for models without the spde when compared with the model with the spde.

But it's either or..either there is overfitting or the the Stdev for spatial.field is no longer important (zero is included in credibility intervals). What is the best way to overcome this problem?

Kurt

As for your question: There can be cases where the spatial model component is not needed, if there is no spatial (residual) structure in the data. This is hard to say without being able to run your code.

Make sure you also use a good prior for the likelihood parameter.

How do you know that the spatial model is overfitting? If the range is too short you can also play with the prior for the range.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

messages.subject: Is R-INLA able to handle the nested error component estimation?
messages.subject_clean: Is R-INLA able to handle the nested error component estimation?
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone

I am a green hand of applying R-INLA. It seems that INLA is very helpful to handle latent Gaussian models (GLMM, HLM, GAMM, etc.).
I have a unbalanced spatio-temporal panel data set.  The relevant modeling is to apply a nested error component regression model.

EX:

y_{ijt}=x_{ijt}+u_{ijt}      i=1,..,M ; j=1,..,N ; t=1,...T
where y_{ijt} could denote the output of the j th firm in the i th industry for the tt h time period. x_{ijt} denotes a vector of k non-stochastic inputs.

The disturbance is given by
u_{ijt}=\mu _{i}+v_{ij}+\varepsilon _{ijt}     i=1,..,M ; j=1,..,N ; t=1,...T

messages.body_plain:
I have count data with has 20% zeros. I would like to use the zeroinflatedpoisson0 model. The zero probability p and poisson mean lambda will be both modeled by some variables, including CAR prior, rw2, etc. The manual for zero-inflated Poisson includes an advanced use of  zeroinflatedpoisson0 to show how to model the probability. Basically, the binary response 0 and 1 follows binomial, and the positive count y follows a Poisson distribution. Since there is no truncated Poisson, the manual used
list(hyper = list(prob = list(initial = -20,fixed = TRUE))
to address the problem with zeroinflatedpoisson0 likelihood.

My problem is: The manual used a single inla function to fit the augmented data, which is stacked by 0-1 responses and positive y, with NA filled in for corresponding covariates. However, when I was searching for the use of zeroinflatedpoisson0, I noticed someone first fit the binomial, then fit the Poisson separately. These two process yield the same result.

Is that always true? Here is the code copied from some post in this email list.

n <- 300
x1 <- rnorm(n)
x2 <- rnorm(n)
x3 <- rnorm(n)

summary(p1 <- plogis(2 +0.5*x1 -2*x2))
summary(mu.pos <- exp(1 -0.5*x1 +1*x3))

table(z <- rbinom(n, 1, p1))
summary(y <- ifelse(z==1, rpois(n, mu.pos), NA))
tapply(y, z, summary)

table(iy0 <- (z==1) & (y==0)) ### where y is zero and z is 1
while(sum(iy0)>0) { ## truncating
  y[iy0] <- rpois(sum(iy0), mu.pos[iy0])
  iy0 <- (z==1) & (y==0)
}
tapply(y, z, summary)

library(INLA)

### model separately
res.z <- inla(z ~ x1 + x2 + x3, 'binomial', data=list(x1=x1, x2=x2, x3=x3, z=z))
res.y <- inla(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, 'zeroinflatedpoisson0',
              data=list(x1=x1, x2=x2, x3=x3, y=y),
              control.family=list(hyper=list(theta=list(intial=10, fixed=TRUE))))
round(cbind(c(2,.5,-2,0), res.z$summary.fix[, 1:5]), 4)
round(cbind(c(1,-.5,0,1), res.y$summary.fix[, 1:5]), 4)

### model jointly
dat <- list(Y=rbind(cbind(z, NA), cbind(NA, y)))
dat$az <- rep(1:0, c(n, n))
dat$x1z <- c(x1, rep(0, n))
dat$x2z <- c(x2, rep(0, n))
dat$x3z <- c(x3, rep(0, n))
dat$ay <- rep(0:1, c(n, n))
dat$x1y <- c(rep(0, n), x1)
dat$x2y <- c(rep(0, n), x2)
dat$x3y <- c(rep(0, n), x3)

res.zy <- inla(Y ~ 0 + az + x1z + x2z + x3z + ay + x1y + x2y + x3y,
               family=c('binomial', 'zeroinflatedpoisson0'), data=dat,
               control.family=list(list(),
                                   list(hyper=list(theta=list(intial=10, fixed=TRUE)))))

round(cbind(true=c(2, .5,-2,0, 1,-.5,0,1),
            res.zy$summary.fix[, 1:5]), 4)

Hi,

I was trying to replicated the spatio-tempo models in the paper
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00477-017-1405-0
The spatio model used is the Leroux CAR model, which has a precision matrix
D =lambda*Q+(1-lambda)* I
This model is expressed using "generic1" latent model. When assigning prior for the mixing parameter lambda, the paper constructed its own uniform (beta) prior as:
lunif = "expression:
a=1;
b=1;
beta = exp(theta)/(1 + exp(theta));
logdens = lgamma(a + b)-lgamma(a)-lgamma(b) + (a-1)*beta + (b-1)*(1-beta);
log_jacobian = log(beta*(1-beta));
return(logdens + log_jacobian)"

log_jacobian = log(beta*(1-beta));return(logdens + log_jacobian)] evaluate to INF or NAN [-1.#INF] for x=38.4912
When x is large, like 38.4912, the beta is actually 1 and the log_jacobian is INF.
Is there any way working around this?

After checking available priors, it seems
beta=list(prior='logitbeta', param=c(1,1))
is exactly the prior above. Is that correct? If so, what is the advantage of using the self-defined prior?

Best,

Jiang

If you have multiple observations in each area, its a matter of modelling.  If you observe the *same* field multiple times, then you can just replicate id.area, like

id.area = c(…, 3,3, ….)

And same with ‘x’

If you have observations of also another realisation of the field, then you can use replicate, to get another field with the same hypearparameters. Like

id.area = c(1:n, 1:n)
r=rep(1:2, each=n)
And then f(id.area, model=“besag”, replicate=r)

Like if you have annual data, and replicate is the annual random effect.

y_{itj} ~ Poisson (mu_{itj})
log(mu_{itj}) = alpha + s_i + d_t + e_{itj}

messages.body_plain:
Both models have the same math. The main difference is that INLA
estimates a high precision/low variance for the random effect with
default prior. Using a more informative prior yields similar results
as lme4

library(INLA)
library(lme4)
sleepstudy$ID <- as.factor(sleepstudy$Subject)

mod1 <- lmer(Reaction ~ 1 + Days + (1 | Subject), sleepstudy)

mod2 <- inla(

  Reaction ~ 1 + Days + f(Subject, model = 'iid'),

  data = sleepstudy,
  control.compute = list(waic = TRUE)
)
mod3 <- inla(

  Reaction ~ 1 + Days +

    f(Subject, model = 'iid', hyper = list(theta = list(param = c(1, 1e-3)))),
  data = sleepstudy,
  control.compute = list(waic = TRUE)
)
par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
plot(
  ranef(mod1)$Subject[, 1],
  mod2$summary.random$Subject$mean
)
abline(a = 0, b = 1)
plot(
  ranef(mod1)$Subject[, 1],
  mod3$summary.random$Subject$mean
)
abline(a = 0, b = 1)

Yes, the problem is in the priors. Yet, the estimates of variances from Thierry are still off from lme4.

You also need to adjust the prior for the precision of the observations (i.e. the residual variance).

The default priors used by INLA are no good here (they are designed for data varying around 1. Your data varies in the hundreds (sd ~ 57). Yet, the default priors for the standard deviations of the data and the Subject effect have 98% of its mass between 0.0034 and 0.069!!!

If instead you adjust your priors so that the 98% central quantile is, for example, between 10 and 200, then you get very similar (point) estimates.

I've put together some code demonstrating this in detail, if you are interested [1]

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Smooth functions like GAMs
messages.body_plain:
The INLA models _are_ GAMs, so I think their wording is a bit unfortunate. I think what you’re really asking is whether the smoothing models in specific frequentist GAM software have correspondences in the R-INLA software, and the answer is yes.
 rw1,ar1, correspond to 1st order spline penalty models, and rw2 corresponds to 2nd order splines.  The main difference is that in frequentist methods it’s mostly the penalized likelihood mode that’s considered, and in Bayesian methods there is a greater emphasis on the Gaussian process aspect of the models.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Brief answer: there are two separate issues: which specific parameterisation to use, and how to simulate from the resulting model. For the simulation part, you will need to construct the precision matrix (easy if you have the graph as an adjacency matrix, and use the standard cholesky method to sample (or just call inla.qsample() if you can use the inla package).

See http://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~flindgre/tmp/gmrf.pdf for details on the computational methods (it doesn’t discuss the necessary graph reordering details though; in inla, they are accessible through inla.qreoreding ) for sampling and conditioning.  The Rue and Held 2005 book on GMRFs is a good source for understanding GMRFs.

Finn

Independent weights for the basis functions only gives the right model if the basis functions were constructed to allow that. It’s possible that the basis functions you can extract from mgcv are like that, but in general this is not true; for example, the whole point of the spde/GMRF representations is that the smoothing property lies in the joint distribution of the weights, for iced, local, basis functions.
The type of smoother that is based on relatively local basis functions and independent weights is heavily dependent on the number of basis functions (leading to the problem of selecting the number of basis functions (or number of spline knots as a model selection problem). Finn

> So by constr=TRUE, the overall sum to zero constraint was added. The
> other constraints were added by extraconstr argument.
>
> So how should I use those information to scale my matrix Rin generic0
> model(I want to use PC prior)?

To use 'inla.scale.model', you have to define the 'constr' argument,
which defines the null space. I think this is what you do in your code.
This approach will work for models of large/huge size, since we can
'correct' for the constraints.

There is also an easier approach, which works (only) for smaller
models, which is just computing the generalized inverse (an O(n^3)
operation which we normally try to avoid), and even more robust, if you
know the rank deficiency, like this

> Q = INLA:::inla.rw <http://inla.rw>(10, order = 2)
> S = INLA:::inla.ginv(Q, rankdef = 2)
> exp(mean(log(diag(S))))
[1] 1.818652956

and then you can scale it with 's'

> s = exp(mean(log(diag(S))))
> Q = s * Q
> S = INLA:::inla.ginv(Q, rankdef = 2)
> exp(mean(log(diag(S))))
[1] 1

> 1. Is that the correct way doing the job?

Yes, you have to add all the constraints in 'constr' when calling
inla.scale.model

> Q = INLA:::inla.rw <http://inla.rw>(10, order = 2)
> constr = list(A = rbind(rep(1,10), 1:10), e = c(0,0))
> QQ = inla.scale.model(Q, constr)
> QQ[1,1] / Q[1]
[1] 1.818650644

the 'same' scaling factor applied.

> 2. I noticed the rank of R.scaled is the same as R. Should I fit the
> scaled model using the same formular like
> ...~ ...+f(ID.area.year, model="generic0", Cmatrix=R.scaled, rankdef=

> r.def, constr=TRUE, hyper=list(prec=list(prior=<some
> prior>), extraconstr=list(A=A.constr, e=rep(0, S+T))))

you can if you like, but this depends on your model.
at least, give the 'rankdef' as there
is no way to know this without doing an expensive calculation.
if you want to lock-down the null-space, you have to
use the (extra)constr like this. you can also
set constr=F and add the sum-to-zero constr in 'extraconstr' (otherwise, it is added
internally)

Best
H

ch.3 in the GMRF book.

is NOT scaled as the marginal variance is 1/(1-\phi^2)/\kappa

in this case, we reparameterize it to be scaled, see inla.doc("ar1")

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

for river network data, one might consider 1D GRMFs linked at the
points where streams join.  But there might be effects that are linked
to more general spatial features, and for those a regular 2D Matern
model can be suitable. A completem model might therefore be a
combination of both types of models.  How to do this in general is an
open research problem, but I think there have been some recent papers
dealing with this (but not necessarily in an INLA context).  I don't
have the references handy, but I believe people in Switzerland were
involved, either from EPFL (possibly Anthony Davison) or ETH (or
both!). I think Marian Scott (and/or others from Glasgow) has been
doing some work in this direction as well.  I'm also working on this
problem with others, but nothing available yet.

Finn
